title: June 2009 (Paper II)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (50/50 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Robert Southey
items.stem:
In a 1817 review of Coleridge’s Biographia Literaria, Francis Jeffrey coined the term
‘Lake School of Poets’ rouping...
items.explanation: Francis Jeffrey, editor of the Edinburgh Review, coined the term 'Lake School of Poets' in his 1817 review of Coleridge's Biographia Literaria to group William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and Robert Southey, who resided in the Lake District.

items.title: Q2 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Wilfred Owen
items.stem:
“I am the enemy you killed, my friend/I knew you in this dark...”
The above lines are taken from...
items.explanation: The haunting lines 'I am the enemy you killed, my friend / I knew you in this dark: for so you frowned / Yesterday through me as you jabbed and killed' occur in Wilfred Owen's celebrated WWI dream poem 'Strange Meeting'.

items.title: Q3 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · William Golding, Derek Walcott, Shashi Tharoor, Jean Rhys
items.stem:
Below are two sets of texts one of which has inspired the other.  Match the text with its
inspiration :
(i)
Coral Island
(ii)
The Odyssey
(iii)
The Mahabharat
(iv)
Jane Eyre
(v)
The Great Indian Novel
(vi)
Wide Sargasso Sea
(vii)
Omeroos
(viii),Lord of the Flies
items.explanation: R. M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island inspired William Golding's Lord of the Flies; Homer's Odyssey inspired Derek Walcott's Omeros; the epic Mahabharata inspired Shashi Tharoor's The Great Indian Novel; and Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre inspired Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea.

items.title: Q4 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
“His life was entle and the elements/So mixed in him, that Nature might stand
up/And say to all the world, ‘This was a man !”’
Who is the speaker, and about whom is this spoken ?
items.explanation: Spoken by Mark Antony over the dead body of Brutus at the conclusion of William Shakespeare's Julius Caesar (Act 5, Scene 5): 'His life was gentle, and the elements / So mixed in him that Nature might stand up / And say to all the world, "This was a man!"' (In the printed exam paper, Option D was credited).

items.title: Q5 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit II: Poetry · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
“When my love swears that she is made of truth/I do believe her, though I know
she lies”.
The author of these lines is...
items.explanation: The opening lines 'When my love swears that she is made of truth / I do believe her, though I know she lies' belong to William Shakespeare's Sonnet 138 (from the 'Dark Lady' sequence).

items.title: Q6 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: The poetry of Wordsworth and Coleridge was notably influenced by...
items.explanation: The early romantic poetry and radical democratic ideals of William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge were profoundly shaped by the political, intellectual, and social ferment of the French Revolution (1789).

items.title: Q7 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden
items.stem:
“Great wits are sure to madness near allied
And thin partitions do their bounds divide”.
The above lines appear in...
items.explanation: In John Dryden's political verse satire Absalom and Achitophel (1681), the famous couplet 'Great wits are sure to madness near allied, / And thin partitions do their bounds divide' characterizes the treacherous Earl of Shaftesbury (Achitophel).

items.title: Q8 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
items.stem: Who among the following developed the term strategic essentialism ?
items.explanation: Postcolonial feminist theorist Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak introduced the term 'strategic essentialism' in the 1980s to describe how subaltern or minority groups temporarily mobilize essentialist identity claims for political solidarity and tactical resistance.

items.title: Q9 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · David Malouf, Ovid
items.stem: David Malouf’s An Imaginary Life is a retelling of the story of :
items.explanation: Australian novelist David Malouf's lyrical novel An Imaginary Life (1978) retells the Roman poet Ovid's exile on the Black Sea coast at Tomis and his transformative spiritual relationship with a feral Child.

items.title: Q10 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Lewis Carroll
items.stem: ‘Jabberwocky’ is a character in....
items.explanation: The Jabberwock (and the famous nonsense ballad 'Jabberwocky') is discovered by Alice in Lewis Carroll's children's fantasy novel Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There (1871).

items.title: Q11 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Edward Said
items.stem:
Which of the following statements is the most accurate regarding Edward Said’s thesis
in Orientalism ?
(i)
The Europeans used the East dialectically to describe their self-image as irrational
and primitive.
(ii)
The Oriental people used the West dialectically to define their self-image as
irrational and primitive.
(iii)
The Europeans used the East oppositionally to define their self-image as rational
and modern.
(iv)
The Oriental people used the West oppositionally to define their self-image as
rational and modern.
items.explanation: In Orientalism (1978), Edward Said argues that European colonial culture used the Orient oppositionally as a negative foil (irrational, sensual, static) to construct Europe's own self-image as rational, enlightened, and modern.

items.title: Q12 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Keats, Thomas Carlyle

items.title: Q13 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Everyman is...
options: a medieval play based on an episode from the Bible
items.explanation: The Somonyng of Everyman (commonly known simply as Everyman, c. 1500) is the most famous surviving English late medieval morality play, using allegorical characters to examine the salvation of the Christian soul.

items.title: Q14 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin, Elizabeth Jennings, John Wain
items.stem: Which of the following sets would you call the poets of the Movement ?
options: Elizabeth Jennings, Philip Larkin, John Wain
W.H. Auden, Cecil Day Lewis, Stephen Spender
T.S. Eliot, Richard Aldington, Ezra Pound
Alan Brownjohn, C.H. Sisson, Anthony Thwaite
items.explanation: The Movement was a 1950s British group of anti-romantic, restrained poets anthologized in Robert Conquest's New Lines (1956), featuring Elizabeth Jennings, Philip Larkin, John Wain, Kingsley Amis, and Donald Davie.

items.title: Q15 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Doris Lessing
items.stem: Doris Lessing’s interest in __________ is widely recognized :
items.explanation: Nobel laureate Doris Lessing had a well-documented lifelong engagement with Sufi mysticism, influenced by her close friendship and study with the Sufi teacher Idries Shah from the 1960s onwards.

items.title: Q16 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Periphrasis, which is a roundabout way of speech/writing, is also known as...
items.explanation: Periphrasis (also known as circumlocution) is a rhetorical figure in which an author uses indirect, roundabout phrasing or multiple words to express an idea that could be stated more directly.

items.title: Q17 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · William Shakespeare, William Caxton
items.stem:
Arrange the following in chronological order...
(i)
The death of Shakespeare
(ii)
Accession of James I to the English throne
(iii)
Caxton and the printing press
(iv)
The Norman Conquest of England
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence is: (iv) The Norman Conquest (1066) -> (iii) William Caxton establishing the printing press at Westminster (1476) -> (ii) Accession of King James I (1603) -> (i) Death of William Shakespeare (1616).

items.title: Q18 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Derek Walcott
items.stem: “The Muse of History” is a classic postcolonial essay by :
items.explanation: 'The Muse of History' (1974) is a seminal postcolonial essay by Saint Lucian poet and playwright Derek Walcott, rejecting linear, bitter colonial recrimination in favor of creative amnesia and artistic regeneration.

items.title: Q19 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Walt Whitman
items.stem:
“Do I contradict myself ?
Very well then, I contradict myself,
(I am large, I contain multitudes.)”
The above lines are from...
items.explanation: The celebrated lines 'Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)' occur in Section 51 of Walt Whitman's foundational American free-verse epic 'Song of Myself' (Leaves of Grass, 1855).

items.title: Q20 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit II: Poetry · Jonathan Swift
items.stem: “Verses on the Death of Dr Swift” was written by...
items.explanation: 'Verses on the Death of Dr. Swift, D.S.P.D.' (1731, published 1739) is a brilliant satirical mock-elegy composed by Jonathan Swift himself, meditating on how his friends and enemies will react upon hearing of his death.

items.title: Q21 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Alfred Lord Tennyson, Matthew Arnold
items.stem:
Match the following elegies with the persons for whom they were written :
(i)
‘Lycidas’
(ii)
Arthur Hugh Clough
(iii)
‘Adonais’
(iv)
A.H. Hallam
(v)
In Memoriam
(vi)
Edward King
(vii)
Thyrsis
(viii),Keats
items.explanation: Milton's 'Lycidas' (1637) mourns his Cambridge friend Edward King; Shelley's 'Adonais' (1821) commemorates John Keats; Tennyson's In Memoriam (1850) honors Arthur Henry Hallam; and Arnold's 'Thyrsis' (1865) laments Arthur Hugh Clough.

items.title: Q22 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Toni Morrison
items.stem: Playing in the Dark by Toni Morrison is a series of reflections on :
items.explanation: Toni Morrison's Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Literary Imagination (1992) is a pioneering collection of critical essays exploring how white canonical American writers (Poe, Melville, Cather, Hemingway) constructed whiteness against a fabricated 'Africanist' presence.

items.title: Q23 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: “He’s not the brightest man in the world” is an example of :
items.explanation: The phrase 'He's not the brightest man in the world' employs litotes, using a negative statement to convey an ironic understatement that politely or humorously implies he is foolish or unintelligent.

items.title: Q24 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Hans Robert Jauss
items.stem: The term ‘horizon of expectations’ is associated with...
items.explanation: German reception theorist Hans Robert Jauss coined the influential concept of the 'horizon of expectations' (Erwartungshorizont) in Toward an Aesthetic of Reception (1967), referring to the shared criteria and literary norms readers bring to a text in a given era.

items.title: Q25 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Mary Seacole, Anthony Trollope
items.stem:
The following writers have something in common :
Mary Seacole
J.A. Froude
Mary Kingsley
Anthony Trollope
What is it ?
(i)
They are all Victorians
(ii)
They are all writers of children’s fiction
(iii)
They are all members of one literary uild
(iv)
They are all travel writers
items.explanation: Mary Seacole (Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands), J. A. Froude (Oceana), Mary Kingsley (Travels in West Africa), and Anthony Trollope (The West Indies and the Spanish Main) were all Victorian writers who produced famous travelogues.

items.title: Q26 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: The immediate source of Christopher Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus is...
items.explanation: The immediate direct source for Christopher Marlowe's tragedy Doctor Faustus was the English translation of the anonymous German narrative Historia von D. Johann Fausten (1587), published in London as The History of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus (1592).

items.title: Q27 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · W. B. Yeats, Lady Gregory, J. M. Synge
items.stem: Who among the following were associated with the Irish Dramatic Movement ?
options: Lady Gregory, W.B. Yeats, J.M. Synge
Jonathan Swift, R.B. Sheridan, G.B. Shaw
W.B. Yeats, J.M. Synge, G.B. Shaw
W.B. Yeats, Patrick J. Kavanagh, Seamus Heaney
items.explanation: The Irish Dramatic Movement (which founded the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1904) was spearheaded by Lady Augusta Gregory, William Butler Yeats, and John Millington Synge (with early patron Edward Martyn).

items.title: Q28 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: The term diaspora was originally applied to the following ethnic roup :
items.explanation: The term 'diaspora' (derived from the Greek meaning 'dispersion' or 'scattering') was originally applied historically to the dispersion of the Jewish people outside their ancestral homeland of Israel following the Babylonian and Roman expulsions.

items.title: Q29 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson, Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Who among the following is NOT a ‘University Wit’ ?
items.explanation: The 'University Wits' were late sixteenth-century Cambridge and Oxford-educated playwrights including Christopher Marlowe, Robert Greene, George Peele, Thomas Nashe, John Lyly, and Thomas Lodge. Ben Jonson was not university-educated and belongs to the Jacobean era.

items.title: Q30 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language: Basic concepts, theories and pedagogy. English in Use.
items.stem:
When a person has a wooden leg, we are apt to say, ‘He has a wooden leg’. Now this
wooden leg is...
(i)
literal
(ii)
metaphorical
(iii)
ambiguous
(iv)
neither literal nor metaphorical
items.explanation: In linguistics and semantics, when someone literally possesses a prosthetic artificial leg made of wood, the term 'wooden leg' is completely literal (designating the physical object itself), rather than a metaphor.

items.title: Q31 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Prosody studies :
items.explanation: Prosody is the formal study of poetic meter, versification, rhythm, stress patterns, and stanzaic forms in verse.

items.title: Q32 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit I: Drama · John Webster
items.stem: Which of the following is a major Jacobean play ?
items.explanation: John Webster's revenge tragedy The Duchess of Malfi was written and performed in 1613–14 during the reign of King James I, making it one of the towering masterworks of Jacobean drama.

items.title: Q33 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks, Robert Penn Warren
items.stem:
Understanding Poetry used to be a classic textbook that encapsulates the principles
of ...
items.explanation: Understanding Poetry (1938), edited by Cleanth Brooks and Robert Penn Warren, became the landmark college textbook that disseminated the pedagogical principles and close-reading methodology of American New Criticism.

items.title: Q34 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
What century is variously called The Age of Enlightenment, the Age of Sensibility.  The
Augustan Age and The Age of Prose and Reason ?
items.explanation: The eighteenth century (1700–1800) in English literary history is variously known as the Age of Enlightenment, the Augustan Age (Age of Pope), the Age of Sensibility (Age of Johnson), and the Neo-Classical Period.

items.title: Q35 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth, Percy Bysshe Shelley, John Keats, Lord Byron
items.stem:
What is common to the following poems ?
Wordsworth’s “The Recluse”
Shelley’s “The Triumph of Life”
Byron’s “Don Juan”
Keats’ “Hyperion”
options: They are all divided into cantos
items.explanation: William Wordsworth's 'The Recluse', Percy Bysshe Shelley's 'The Triumph of Life', John Keats's 'Hyperion', and Lord Byron's 'Don Juan' are all renowned Romantic masterworks that were left unfinished at their authors' deaths.

items.title: Q36 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: Who among the following called the novel ‘the bright book of life’ ?
items.explanation: In his essay 'Why the Novel Matters' (1925), D. H. Lawrence famously proclaimed that 'the novel is the one bright book of life', ranking it above science, philosophy, and scripture because it portrays human life in its living, dynamic wholeness.

items.title: Q37 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: “Ripeness is all” is a line from...
items.explanation: The stoic line 'Men must endure / Their going hence, even as their coming hither: / Ripeness is all' is spoken by Edgar to his blind father Gloucester in Shakespeare's King Lear (Act 5, Scene 2).

items.title: Q38 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · U. R. Ananthamurthy, A. K. Ramanujan
items.stem: U.R. Ananthamurthy’s Samskara was translated by...
items.explanation: U. R. Ananthamurthy's landmark modernist Kannada novel Samskara: A Rite for a Dead Brahmin (1965) was translated into an acclaimed English edition by poet and scholar A. K. Ramanujan in 1976.

items.title: Q39 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Abel Whittle is a character in :
items.explanation: Abel Whittle is the illiterate, put-upon rustic workman in Thomas Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886) who, despite being publicly humiliated by Michael Henchard, faithfully cares for Henchard in his lonely final days.

items.title: Q40 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: In which eclogue of The Shepheardes Calender does Spenser praise Queen Elizabeth I ?
items.explanation: In Edmund Spenser's pastoral calendar poem The Shepheardes Calender (1579), the 'April' eclogue features Colin Clout's sumptuous song of praise celebrating Queen Elizabeth I as 'Elisa, Queen of shepherds all'.

items.title: Q41 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT the opening of the well-known Romantic poem ?
options: My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains/My sense
Margaret, are you rieving/Over Goldengrove unleaving ?
The world is too much with us
items.explanation: 'Margaret, are you grieving / Over Goldengrove unleaving?' is the opening couplet of Victorian Jesuit poet Gerard Manley Hopkins's poem 'Spring and Fall' (written 1880), whereas the other choices open Romantic poems by Keats, Shelley, and Wordsworth.

items.title: Q42 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · George Orwell
items.stem: “Politics and the English Language” is an essay by :
items.explanation: George Orwell published his influential critical essay 'Politics and the English Language' in April 1946 in Horizon, critiquing ugly, vague, and dishonest political prose and outlining six rules for clarity in writing.

items.title: Q43 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake
items.stem: “The mind-forged manacles” is phrase from :
items.explanation: The powerful phrase 'In every cry of every Man, / In every Infant's cry of fear, / In every voice, in every ban, / The mind-forg'd manacles I hear' occurs in William Blake's poem 'London' from Songs of Experience (1794).

items.title: Q44 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Matthew Arnold, William Wordsworth
items.stem:
“He is not fully recognized at home; he is not recognized at all abroad.  Yet I firmly
believe that the poetical performance of __________ is, after that of Shakespeare and
Milton, undoubtedly most considerable in our language.”
To whom does Matthew Arnold refer in the above statement ?
items.explanation: In his 1879 essay on William Wordsworth (included in Essays in Criticism: Second Series), Matthew Arnold declared that despite lack of full continental recognition, Wordsworth's poetic performance was the greatest in English after Shakespeare and Milton.

items.title: Q45 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: The Globe Theatre opened in :
items.explanation: The original Globe Theatre was built in 1599 in Southwark on the south bank of the River Thames by Shakespeare's playing company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

items.title: Q46 · June 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Tzvetan Todorov
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions (46 to 50):

We need to begin by casting doubt on the legitimacy of the notion of literature. The mere fact that the word exists, or that an academic institution has been built around it, does not mean that the thing itself is self-evident.
Reasons—perfectly empirical ones, to begin with—are not hard to find. The full history of the word literature and its equivalents in all languages and all eras has yet to be written, but even a perfunctory look at the question makes it clear that the term has not been around for ever. In the European languages, the word literature in its current sense is quite recent: it dates back—just barely—to the nineteenth century. Might we be dealing with a historical phenomenon rather than an "eternal" one? Moreover, many languages (many African languages, for example) have no generic term covering all literary productions. To these initial observations we may add the fragmentation characteristic of literature today. Who dares specify what is literature and what is not, given the irreducible variety of the writing that tends to be attached to it, from vastly different perspectives?
The argument is not conclusive: a notion may legitimately exist even if there is no specific term in the lexicon for it. But we have been led to cast the first shadow of doubt over the "naturalness" of literature. A theoretical examination of the problem proves no more reassuring. Where do we come by the conviction that there is indeed such a thing as literature? From experience. We study "literary" works in school, then in college; we find the "literary" type of book in specialized stores; we are in the habit of referring to "literary" authors in everyday conversation. An entity called "literature" functions at the level of intersubjective and social relations; this much seems beyond question. Fine. But what have we proved? That in the broader system of a given society or culture, an identifiable element exists that is known by the label literature. Have we thereby demonstrated that all the particular products that take on the function of "literature" possess common characteristics, which we can identify with legitimacy? Not at all.

Question 46:
This passage casts doubt on :
items.explanation: The passage begins explicitly by stating: 'We need to begin by casting doubt on the legitimacy of the notion of literature', problematizing literature as a self-evident cultural category.

Question 47:
Literature is unsustainable because :...
options: we are unclear as to what it means.
we are unsure as to its message.
we are not persuaded that the claims made for it are allowable and acceptable.
we cannot prove that its definitions are the right and the only possible ones.
items.explanation: The author argues that simply because a social institution exists does not mean that all products labeled 'literature' possess demonstrable, legitimate common characteristics that justify universal claims.

We study "literary" works in school, then in college; we find the "literary" type of book in specialized stores; we are in the habit of referring to "literary" authors in everyday conversation. An entity called "literature" functions at the level of intersubjective and social relations; this much seems beyond question. Fine. But what have we proved? That in the broader system of a given society or culture, an identifiable element exists that is known by the label literature. Have we thereby demonstrated that all the particular products that take on the function of "literature" possess common characteristics, which we can identify with legitimacy? Not at all.

Question 48:
How does the writer argue that the existence of literature is hardly self-evident ?
(i)
by citing reasons for its non-existence.
(ii)
by citing reasons for interrogating its legitimacy.
(iii)
by citing reasons and proving by argument that its legitimacy can be interrogated.
(iv)
by citing reasons to show that the label does not match the thing we know to be
literature.
items.explanation: The author builds an empirical argument showing that the word literature is historically recent and absent in many languages, thereby proving that its legitimacy must be critically interrogated.

Reasons—perfectly empirical ones, to begin with—are not hard to find. Might we be dealing with a historical phenomenon rather than an "eternal" one? Moreover, many languages (many African languages, for example) have no generic term covering all literary productions. To these initial observations we may add the fragmentation characteristic of literature today. Question 49:
“Might we be dealing with a historical phenomenon rather than an ‘eternal’ one” ?
What makes this a reasonable question to consider in this context ?
options: A historical phenomenon lends itself to better empirical verification than an ‘eternal’ one.
A historical  phenomenon has more legitimacy than an ‘eternal’ one.
A historical phenomenon can be debated and possibly settled while an ‘eternal’ one must be taken on trust or not at all.
A historical phenomenon is well above disputation while an ‘eternal’ one is not.
items.explanation: A historical phenomenon has a documentable timeline and empirical emergence (dating to the nineteenth century), making it subject to historical and linguistic verification unlike a timeless, eternal concept.
